title: Lesson 1 · "Problematical Situations," Not "Problems"
text: Lesson 1 · "Problematical Situations," Not "Problems" Checkland and Poulter deliberately avoid the word "problem." A problem implies a well-defined thing that can be solved out of existence. Real situations in organizations and everyday life are messier than that — so SSM calls them "problematical situations": situations about which someone has the feeling that "something needs to be done about this." The reading's own examples Situation Why it isn't a clean "problem" A company wonders whether to bid for a smaller rival's equity No obviously "correct" answer — it depends on judgment, risk appetite, and whose interests count A university's intake is biased toward middle-class students "Fixing" it raises further open questions about what changing it would actually involve A government wants security from terrorism without losing civil liberties The two goals trade off against each other; there's no single correct balance A local council's services aren't "citizen-friendly" "Citizen-friendly" itself means different things to different people A head teacher decides whether the school or the local authority should run school meals Depends on who benefits from a surplus and how much control matters Notice what all five have in common: each could be tackled by "appealing to previous experience; intuitively; by randomly thrashing about... by responding emotionally" — or by using a genuine method of inquiry. SSM is that method. Common misreading. "Problematical situation" is not just a softer synonym for "problem." The whole point of the word choice is to keep open the possibility that there is no single correct fix — only a situation that different people, with different criteria, experience differently. If you find yourself asking "what's the solution to this problematical situation," you've slipped back into hard-systems thinking without noticing. What "everyday life" actually looks like, per the reading We experience life as an "onrushing turbulent stream, a flux of happenings, ideas, emotions, actions, all mediated through the slippery agency of language, all continually changing." Nothing is intrinsically "a situation" — it is our own perceptions that carve a "situation" out of that flux, and in doing so we already know its boundaries and content will keep changing. This is why SSM is a flexible process , not a fixed technique or a sequence of steps you could hand to a robot. Checkland calls it a methodology rather than a method precisely because "the human world is one in which nothing ever happens twice, not in exactly the same way" — a methodology is a set of principles adapted to each unique situation, not a recipe.

title: Lesson 1 · Worldview and the Core Systems Ideas
text: Lesson 1 · Worldview and the Core Systems Ideas To judge anything as "good" or "bad," you need criteria . Different people's criteria come from different genetic makeup and, above all, different life experience — and over time those criteria firm up into a relatively stable outlook, a worldview (German Weltanschauung ), through which a person perceives the world. The book calls worldview "the most important concept in understanding the complexity of human situations, and indeed, the nature and form of SSM." Worldview lens: same facts, different verdict Pick a scenario, then try each worldview on it. Nothing about the underlying facts changes — only the criteria used to judge them. Scenario: Economic activity (the reading's example) A prison's daily routine (the reading's example) An armed group attacks a government facility (the reading's example) Choose a worldview above. What this does not mean. Neither observer is "factually wrong." Worldviews aren't errors to correct — they're stable, and can change over time (the book's example: "a paranoid person whose worldview is 'this hostile world owes me a living' might become a more integrated member of society as a result of experiencing love and generosity"), but they can't be argued away by pointing at facts both sides already agree on. The four requirements of an adaptive whole (a "system") Systems ideas are the toolkit SSM borrows — but redirected, as the next section explains. The core systems concept is an adaptive whole : something that survives through time by adapting to changes in its environment. Click each requirement to see what it means. E (environment) S SS SS Communication processes Control processes Structure in layers Emergent properties A system S receives shocks from its changing environment E (the arrows). Click a requirement to see why survival depends on it. Select all that apply Which two of these are among the four requirements Figure 1.1 lists for a system S to survive through time? Structure in layers A written objective function Emergent properties A single, unified worldview Check The four are communication processes, control processes, structure in layers, and emergent properties — only two of which appear above. "Objective function" belongs to hard systems engineering, and a "single worldview" is the opposite of what SSM expects to find in a real situation.

title: Lesson 1 · Purposeful Activity Models and the Learning Cycle
text: Lesson 1 · Purposeful Activity Models and the Learning Cycle Every real-world problematical situation — whether "a small firm making wheelbarrows" or a "multi-national oil company" — has one thing in common: it contains people trying to act purposefully , not just acting on instinct. SSM's key move is to treat purposeful action itself as a system — an adaptive whole, built the same way as Figure 1.1, with the "operations" being monitored against defined measures of performance so that control action can be taken. Worked example: painting the garden fence (Fig. 1.2 & 1.3) A logically linked set of activities forms a whole whose emergent property is purposefulness . Arrows show one activity depending on another. 1. Decide the scope of the task → 2. Appraise the colour scheme of the property → 3. Decide colour to paint the fence → 4. Obtain paint 5. Obtain brush 6. Prepare fence for painting → 7. Apply paint to fence 8. Define measures of performance → 9. Monitor activities 1–7 → 10. Take control action Activity 7 (apply paint) depends on 4, 5, and 6 all being done first — that's what the arrows into it mean. Multiple choice Whose worldview does this particular model express? An objective, worldview-free description of fence painting The householder's: "I can do useful DIY jobs to improve my property" The neighbour's worldview about property upkeep The paint manufacturer's worldview The model is built entirely within the fence-painter's own worldview . The book is explicit that other relevant worldviews exist even in a case this trivial — the neighbours' or a partner's — and each would require a different model, since a model can only ever encapsulate one pure worldview at a time. The single most-missed idea in the whole reading. Purposeful activity models can never be descriptions of (part of) the real world. Each one expresses only one way of looking at the situation, and there will always be multiple possibilities (think of the Olympics example: the IOC, the host city, athletes, sponsors, security staff, and a group seeking publicity for a cause could each need a different relevant model — "there could never be a single model relevant to all these different interests"). A model's job is to be a device — an intellectual tool that generates good questions about the real situation, not a picture of it. The learning cycle (Fig. 1.4 & 1.5) Once you have models built from different worldviews, you use them as a source of questions : does real activity in the situation look more, or less, like the model? Should it? That comparison structures a real discussion/debate whose purpose is to surface different worldviews and find an accommodation — a version of the situation different people, with different worldviews, could nevertheless live with . A candidate change has to clear two bars simultaneously: Bar Meaning Arguably desirable Justified by what using the models to question the situation revealed Culturally feasible Workable for these particular people, given their particular history and politics — not a generic "best practice" The four stages, as the classic diagram (Fig. 1.5) shows them: (1) find out about the perceived real-world problematical situation, (2) build purposeful activity models relevant to it (each based on a declared worldview), (3) use the models to structure a discussion about change, and (4) define/take action to improve. Common misreading: the cycle is not a checklist you complete once, in order. The book says this explicitly: describing the cycle as steps 1–4 "may give a false impression that we are describing a sequence of steps. Not so." In real use (Fig. 1.6), finding-out runs continuously, model-building happens in bursts fed by both the models and the ongoing finding-out, and discussion feeds back into more finding-out and more modelling. It is, in principle, never-ending : taking action changes the situation into a new one, which the cycle can address all over again. LUMAS: how a user actually applies the methodology LUMAS = L earning for a U ser by a M ethodology-informed A pproach to a S ituation. Read it starting from the user (U) in the centre: perceiving a problematical situation (S) and appreciating the methodology (M), the user tailors M to S to produce a specific approach (A) for this situation. Using A doesn't just improve the situation — it also yields learning (L) , which can in turn modify how the user appreciates the methodology itself. Fill in the LUMAS acronym: L earning for a by a -informed to a Check all Learning for a User by a Methodology -informed Approach to a Situation . It is a generic model of how any methodology (not just SSM) gets tailored to a unique real situation by the person using it.

title: Lesson 1 · Hard vs. Soft Systems Thinking
text: Lesson 1 · Hard vs. Soft Systems Thinking SSM grew out of Systems Engineering (SE) — developed at Bell Telephone — which names a "system" (assumed to exist, or be buildable, in the real world), defines its objectives, then engineers it to meet them. SE was found "poverty-stricken" for human situations: "too thin, not rich enough to deal with fizzing social complexity." The fix was not to add more technique — it was to change where "systemicity" is assumed to live. Observer 1 — "hard" "I spy systems which I can engineer." The world itself is taken to contain systems with fixed objectives. This is the stance of Systems Engineering, classical Operational Research, the Viable System Model, and early System Dynamics — none of which have a place for conflicting worldviews. Observer 2 — "soft" "I spy complexity and confusion; but I can organize exploration of it as a learning system." The social world itself is complex, problematical, and mysteriously shot through with clashing worldviews — created and recreated by people thinking, talking, and acting. What's systemic is the process of inquiry , not the world being inquired into. Common misreading. "Hard vs. soft" is not "quantitative vs. qualitative," and it isn't a value judgment about rigor. It's a question of where the word "system" is allowed to attach : to the world itself (hard), or only to the inquiry process built to make sense of the world (soft). This is also why casual, everyday talk of "the education system" or "the healthcare system" is a trap — SSM's technical sense of "system" never refers to those real-world chunks directly, only to models and the inquiry process. True / False In SSM, "the prison system" is itself a system in the technical sense the methodology uses. True False Everyday language uses "system" loosely, to mean "a complex chunk of reality that might be better engineered." SSM's technical use is much narrower: systemicity belongs to the models (each built from one declared worldview) and to the process of inquiry — never directly to a real-world institution. True / False Hard systems thinking and soft systems thinking mainly differ over whether to use numbers. True False They differ over where systemicity is located — in the world (hard) or in the process of inquiry into the world (soft) — not over quantitative versus qualitative method. Match the stance to its belief Systems Engineering (hard) — choose — Systems exist in the world and can be engineered to meet fixed objectives The world is complex and contested; the inquiry process itself can be organized as a learning system SSM (soft) — choose — Systems exist in the world and can be engineered to meet fixed objectives The world is complex and contested; the inquiry process itself can be organized as a learning system Check

title: Lesson 1 · What a Rich Picture Is (and Isn't) — Preview
text: Lesson 1 · What a Rich Picture Is (and Isn't) — Preview Where this fits. The assigned reading for this meeting (the Preamble and Chapter 1) lays the conceptual groundwork — problematical situations, worldview, purposeful activity models, the learning cycle — but doesn't itself walk through how to draw a rich picture. That's a "finding out" technique detailed in Chapter 2, which isn't assigned yet. What follows previews the idea from the syllabus's own framing so today's class makes sense; expect the full technique (symbols, drawing conventions, worked examples) once Chapter 2 is assigned. The course's own framing: "Human situations are complex because they always involve multiple interacting relationships. A picture shows those relations all at once, which a paragraph can only deliver one after another: that is the whole argument for drawing one." What a rich picture is A way of capturing a problematical situation's structure (roles, physical layout, reporting lines) and process (what actually happens, who does what) together, at a glance. A "finding out" device — it belongs to stage (1) of the learning cycle, before any purposeful activity model gets built. Meant to surface tensions, concerns, and multiple worldviews simultaneously — exactly the kind of thing a paragraph of prose has to present one sentence at a time, losing the "all at once" quality that makes interacting relationships visible. What it is not Not this Why not A flowchart A flowchart shows a sequence of steps toward one outcome; a rich picture shows many relationships coexisting, with no single "flow" An org chart An org chart shows only formal reporting lines; a rich picture also shows informal tensions, physical realities, and concerns an org chart can't represent Judged as art Its purpose is to communicate structure and process to the people in the situation, not to be aesthetically impressive Multiple choice Which best describes why Checkland & Poulter's tradition uses a picture rather than a paragraph to capture a problematical situation? Pictures are quicker to draw than paragraphs A picture looks more professional in a report A picture can show multiple interacting relationships all at once, where prose can only present them one after another A picture avoids the need to talk to people in the situation The stated argument is entirely about simultaneity : complex human situations always involve multiple interacting relationships, and only a picture can show them together rather than one-after-another the way sentences must. True / False A rich picture is essentially a flowchart of the main process in a situation. True False The course materials explicitly rule this out: a rich picture is "not a flowchart, not an org chart, and not judged as art." A flowchart's sequential, single-outcome shape is exactly what a rich picture is meant to avoid.

title: Lesson 2 · Information Systems Start with Purposeful Activity
text: Lesson 2 · Information Systems Start with Purposeful Activity Mon Oct 5 · "Systems worth thinking with" · Ch.4, pp.111–114. The unit's slogan: a relevant system is a choice of viewpoint; a model that tries to be balanced argues for nothing. Chapter 4 opens with a claim about why SSM belongs in information-systems work : as soon as you have an activity model, you can ask of each activity in it — What information would have to be available to someone carrying this out? What information would doing it generate? (then: who supplies or uses it, in what form, how often). So an activity model can be turned into an information model (p.111). The questions you ask of the real world become information-oriented. Data → capta → information → knowledge (Fig. 4.1) There are "uncountable millions of facts about the world" — data . The temperature at Reykjavik airport right now is undoubtedly recorded somewhere, but we have no interest in it — until we are flying to Iceland tomorrow and about to pack. Then it becomes "an item of data which we have an interest in knowing ." English has no word for that distinction, so Checkland and Holwell suggest capta (Latin capere , "to take") for the subset of data we pay attention to. Click each stage: Data Capta Information Knowledge Common misreading. "Information" is not something a computer holds. The reading's line is blunt: information is created "when human beings attribute meaning to data in a particular context. No machine operations can do that." A designer "cannot determine how the system will be used" — the example is a spreadsheet of student marks that "ostensibly provides information concerning student assessment" but which lecturers "may well use … in internal battles over uneven teaching loads!" (p.113). Machines manipulate electronic tokens for data; people confer meaning. Multiple choice In the Reykjavik example, what turns an ordinary datum (the airport temperature) into capta ? It is stored in a database A computer processes it into a report Someone takes an interest in knowing it (here, because they are about to travel there) A second source confirms it Capta is "that subset of all data which we have an interest in knowing." What changes is the person's interest , not the data and not the storage. Context then turns capta into information . True / False According to the reading, a sufficiently well-designed system can itself create information from data. True False Information is created when human beings attribute meaning to data in a particular context — "no machine operations can do that." The system designer has some information provision in mind, but cannot control how it will be used (p.113). Match each term to its meaning Data — choose — Facts about the world, whether or not anyone cares about them The subset of data we have an interest in knowing Capta made meaningful by a context and by the person's interests Larger, longer-living structures of meaningful facts Capta — choose — Facts about the world, whether or not anyone cares about them The subset of data we have an interest in knowing Capta made meaningful by a context and by the person's interests Larger, longer-living structures of meaningful facts Information — choose — Facts about the world, whether or not anyone cares about them The subset of data we have an interest in knowing Capta made meaningful by a context and by the person's interests Larger, longer-living structures of meaningful facts Knowledge — choose — Facts about the world, whether or not anyone cares about them The subset of data we have an interest in knowing Capta made meaningful by a context and by the person's interests Larger, longer-living structures of meaningful facts Check IS vs. IT: design the activity first (Fig. 4.2) "No one creates an information system for its own sake." An IS exists because it helps, supports, or enables someone carrying out some purposeful activity . And "when one system, A, supports another, B, it is obvious that you cannot conceptualize or design A until you have first conceptualized B" (pp.113–114). So if a managing director asks for a system to support research, you cannot move until you know what "research support" means to that company . Real-world purposeful activity ↑ supports Information Systems (IS) ↑ enables Information Technology (IT) …and IT can yield ideas for new IS or new activity (the dotted arrows) "Especially to be avoided is the procurement of a complex IT system without first thinking out exactly how it will be used, as well as what activity it will serve" (p.114). Case 3 later reports the bill for skipping that step: seven of 150 RM systems were "procured but not installed" (p.135). The dotted arrows matter too: modern IT "may make possible purposeful activity and information systems which would be impossible without it," so the arrow runs both ways — but sensible thinking still starts from the activity. Multiple choice Which description matches Figure 4.2? IT supports the purposeful activity, which in turn enables the IS The IS supports real-world purposeful activity; IT enables the IS Purposeful activity supports the IS, which enables IT IS, IT and purposeful activity are independent of one another The IS exists to support some purposeful activity, and IT is what enables the IS to be realized. That is why you define the activity first. Multiple choice A managing director asks you to design a system to support the company's research. According to pp.113–114, what must you do first ? Conceptualize what "research support" would mean for that company — the activity being supported Choose the database technology Survey vendors of research software Draft the user-interface screens You cannot design system A (the information system) until you have conceptualized system B (the purposeful activity it supports). Everything else on the list comes after. Fill in the blank: before working on an information system you must first carefully define the purposeful that the system will support. Check Activity. The general message of the setup section: focus on defining carefully the purposeful activity the information system will support.

title: Case 1 · Creating an Information Strategy in an Acute Hospital
text: Case 1 · Creating an Information Strategy in an Acute Hospital Ch.4, pp.115–124. The deck's frame: two hospitals, one deadline . The situation In the early 1990s the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle (a large acute hospital) and Hexham General (much smaller, 25 miles away) merged into one organization while staying on separate sites . The Information Officer of the new hospital, Steve Clarke, used the merger to reformulate the combined information and IT strategy: central NHS money, work put out to tender, a management consultancy (John Poulter), and Checkland brought in for methodological guidance. Work began in March ; the strategy had to reach the Board in September . The plan: about forty professionals — doctors, nurses, people from estates and accounting — in small mixed groups , each examining the core purpose, activities and information needs of some of the hospital's functions; a monthly plenary; a steering group of directors and senior managers. The Chief Executive stressed the strategy would come "not from 'management' but from the work of small groups of hospital professionals." What the groups were given Only two pieces of SSM beyond its general role: CATWOE and the measures of performance for T — E1 efficacy, E2 efficiency, E3 effectiveness (p.117). Plus generic models of "an acute hospital" to adopt or modify. The generic root definition: a system, operating under a range of external influences, which, in the light of a strategy based on its capabilities and costs, delivers services defined in "contracts" with purchasers within the context of NHS norms and policies, that service delivery itself contributing to the ongoing development of its strategy. Its CATWOE and three Es (p.117) Element In the hospital model C Customers those receiving hospital services; purchasers A Actors hospital professionals T Transformation need for acute services → need for acute services met W Worldview acute services can best be provided by an organization dedicated to developing and delivering such services O Owners hospital management board; NHS executive E Environment NHS structures and norms; the purchaser–provider split E1 efficacy demonstrable delivery of a portfolio of services of suitable quality E2 efficiency minimum use of resources (expressible in money and time) E3 effectiveness satisfaction of patients treated, purchasers, the NHS executive; contributions to hospital reputation (long-term viability) The model (Fig. 4.3) had five main activities — "the 'magical number' 7 minus 2 in this case!" — with four expanded at a second level (Fig. 4.4 expands activity 4.1). It is "very rare to expand more than two levels below that of a starting model" (p.120). The course of the project (Fig. 4.5) March Mar–Apr April May–June July–Aug September The trade-off the reading is open about. The tight timescale and the required outcome (a reformulated strategy based on the hospital's current pattern of activity ) meant the work "would focus on primary-task models rather than issue-based ones" (p.116). The deck quotes the outcome section twice: "the timescale dictated that it would be based on existing patterns of hospital activity" (p.121), and "In the time available it could not have become a more luxurious study of future hospital strategy" (pp.121–122) — which would have needed "more models, including ones which were issue-based." A deadline can choose your kind of model before anyone chooses a worldview. The nurse's C (p.123) One group, led by a senior nurse, defined CATWOE for "a system to provide a hospital nursing service" before modifying a generic model. Asked C — who would be the beneficiaries or victims? they said "patients" at once and moved on. A group member pulled them back: under the "internal market" (annual contracts with a purchaser), the C could arguably be the hospital "contracts manager," with the nurses' job being "to supply the amount and quality of nursing care that was paid for under the contract." The ensuing "long and animated discussion" let the senior nurse see why she had felt, without being able to pinpoint it, that the contracting regime was eroding her profession's autonomy. A second moment: a paediatrician said, "I've worked here for 20 years, and this is the first time I've ever had any sense of the total activity of the hospital as a whole" (pp.123–124). The authors' reading: "although no methodology can itself produce learning and 'answers,' as if by magic, organized use of methodological guidelines can render the users' own thinking more coherent and more effective" (p.124). The deck puts the two answers side by side: patients vs. the hospital contracts manager . Same activity, different C — and the choice of C is not neutral. It is a choice of viewpoint. title: Cases 2–4 · Evaluating and Reorganizing
text: Cases 2–4 · Evaluating and Reorganizing Ch.4, pp.124–144. Three more uses of SSM around information systems. Each ends with a lesson about method. Case 2 · Evaluating a clinical information system (pp.124–129) Part of the national Resource Management (RM) Initiative in the NHS (£300m of public money). At Huddersfield, a clinical information system (CIS) had begun without any tight definition of an ultimate aim ; it proceeded at the pace and direction the four consultants involved would accept. SSM was used after the event to describe what had emerged. The expected model was doctors treating patients — but the CIS turned out to be "a system which monitored the taken-as-given 'diagnose and treat' activity, took control action with respect to it, and learned from the experience" (p.126; Fig. 4.6). How it worked: consultants entered an anticipated profile of care for a condition (symptoms, complications, treatments, expected stay, outcomes, plus resource use and costs), recorded actual cases in the same format, and a facilitator ran regular meetings to compare experience with the profiles and modify them. Lesson: desirable changes have to be feasible for these people in their specific situation , with "its own history and sense-making narrative" (p.129). A good IS includes arrangements for capturing learning from its operation, and the key feature was "ongoing joint work by doctors and information professionals" — not designers imposing a system "on apparently awkward and obtuse users, who naturally resist." Case 3 · Evaluating a national initiative (pp.130–136) The evaluation of RM across 250+ projects and £300m. SSM was used twice: SSM(p) — "How shall we go about this investigation?" — and SSM(c) — "How shall we create and then capture the content of this evaluation from the huge mass of material collected?" (p.131). The Health Notice that launched RM (12 pages) was "taken to be an elaborate Root Definition "; three RDs were modelled (set up and execute an RM project; manage one; fund and monitor at regional level) (p.133). Those models structured the questions for 16 four-day site visits , a questionnaire to 200+ sites (130 returned), and about 30 national and regional interviews . To analyse the pile of visit reports, they built an idealised "RM-ed site" that took the Notice "as a sacred text" — an activity model "expressed the other way round": elements are entities and arrows carry activities (Fig. 4.8, pp.133–134). Outcomes: IS and organization-development work were rarely linked , and in seven cases out of 150 systems were "procured but not installed" (p.135) — "the usual results when too early an emphasis on IT neglects prior analysis of the purposeful activity to be supported." Lessons: SSM's verb-based models are usually superior in human affairs, "since function is more important than form — which is arbitrary and can be easily changed." And: "Never dive straight into complex situations. Organize prior thinking about intervention by the use of guiding principles about complexity and frameworks and tools for inquiry" (p.136). Case 4 · Information support for scientists (pp.137–144) In a large multinational science-based company the Information Department (ID: 100 people, serving laboratories of 1,000) wanted to rethink the support it gave researchers. Eva led the project; the initiative came from ID, not from the researchers , who did not hold ID in high esteem. SSM was used with workshops of about 20 researchers: a rich picture (Fig. 4.9), then ID's own mission statement modelled as if it were a root definition (Fig. 4.10). Gaps between such a model and real life "usually appear" because mission statements are "normally part of PR rather than the result of dispassionate thinking" (p.138). Workshop discussion converged on: "what the researcher needs is more important than how ID wants to use technology" (p.139). Then came a hiatus of nearly a year (the reorganization's terms of reference covered only one section of ID), ending in an "Information Market" — a permanent platform for dialogue. Lesson: the SSM work took about half a dozen days; the organizational change "was much, much slower." The head of ID held a "commodity of power" but was reluctant to use it (Analyses Two and Three). "There is never a straightforward, spick and span answer to the question: What is culturally feasible here?" (p.144). the organizational change was far slower than the SSM work Case 2 — Huddersfield CIS — choose — Generic primary-task models used by small mixed groups to build an information strategy to a deadline SSM used after the event to discover that a system monitored the "diagnose and treat" activity and learned from it SSM used to design a large evaluation and to structure its findings with an entity-based model Workshops using a mission-statement model and a rich picture; title: Aspect vs. Relevant System
text: Aspect vs. Relevant System From the Oct 5 deck, with Ch.2 p.38. This is the move your group makes after choosing what to study. Your aspect What you are looking at. One per group. Committed to on 9/14 . A relevant system How you look at it. Several per group, from today onward. The deck's example comes from the first week ( 8/26 ): one subject, two relevant systems . Subject: group work. Relevant system 1 — group work is for producing more, or higher quality, work than is possible individually . Relevant system 2 — group work is a device for producing individual learning . Same subject, different system, because each is built from a different point of view. And: "What is your relevant system?" is not answered by the name of your aspect. One model, one worldview (Ch.2, p.38) "Each model is built according to a declared single worldview (e.g. 'the Olympic Games from the perspective of the host city')." The deck repeats the Games from three other perspectives: an athlete , a broadcaster , and a family moved out to make room for a stadium . Pick a perspective to see why one model per worldview matters (the one-line "working if" statements below are illustrations , not from the reading): Athlete Broadcaster Displaced family A "balanced" model Choose a perspective above. The unit's slogan. "A model that tries to be balanced argues for nothing and can be argued with by no one." If a model tries to satisfy the athlete, the broadcaster and the displaced family at once, nobody can say what it is for — and so nobody can disagree with it. A relevant system is a choice of viewpoint ; the value of a model is that it gives you something definite to argue with. Multiple choice Your aspect is "group work." Which of these is a relevant system for it? "Group work" (the name of the aspect) A system in which group work is a device for producing individual learning A balanced system that serves every stakeholder in group work equally The class's group-work grading policy A relevant system says how you look at the subject, from a stated point of view. The name of the aspect doesn't; a "balanced" system has no single worldview; and a policy is a thing in the world, not a viewpoint. Multiple choice A group builds one "fair" model of the Olympic Games that includes the athlete's, the broadcaster's and the displaced family's views. What is wrong with it? It tries to be balanced, so it argues for nothing and can be argued with by no one Three perspectives take too long to draw Models may only express the host city's view Nothing; balanced models are the goal Each model must be built according to a declared single worldview (Ch.2, p.38). A different perspective gets a different model. True / False Naming your aspect (for example, "advising") is enough to answer "What is your relevant system?" True False The deck says so directly: "What is your relevant system?" is not answered by the name of your aspect. The aspect is what you look at; the relevant system is how.

title: Primary-Task vs. Issue-Based Models
text: Primary-Task vs. Issue-Based Models Ch.2, pp.43–44, as framed in the Oct 5 deck. "Never work with only one kind." Primary-task (PT) The boundary is an existing unit : an office, a committee, a division. Not wrong. But it takes the organization chart as given, and nobody notices . Issue-based (IB) The boundary cuts across the chart . "Questions about what departments, sections, etc. should exist … are always bound up in the power-play." The two candidates every group may take Issue-based: a system to turn unallocated resources into allocated ones (Ch.2, p.44). Primary-task: the school's own mission statement (sdis.unc.edu/about), modelled as if it were a root definition (Ch.4, p.138 — exactly what Case 4 did with ID's mission statement). Case 1 shows how the kind gets chosen by circumstance: a deadline and a required answer (a strategy based on current activity) pushed it to primary-task models. The card exercise (in class on 10/5) Line 1: A system to … (one sentence). Line 2: Who would think this worth doing, and why? (the worldview). Corner: PT or IB. By 2:16: at least eight cards, at least two marked IB, and at least one that nobody at your table holds , marked ✗ (the skeptic makes sure it is written). Then lay them out: two cards with the same line 2? One system — merge them. A card that is the name of your aspect? Not a system yet. A card that tries to please everyone? Split it. Match each term to its meaning Aspect — choose — What you are looking at; one per group How you look at it; several per group, each from one declared worldview Boundary is an existing unit such as an office, committee or division Boundary cuts across the organization chart Relevant system — choose — What you are looking at; one per group How you look at it; several per group, each from one declared worldview Boundary is an existing unit such as an office, committee or division Boundary cuts across the organization chart Primary-task — choose — What you are looking at; one per group How you look at it; several per group, each from one declared worldview Boundary is an existing unit such as an office, committee or division Boundary cuts across the organization chart Issue-based — choose — What you are looking at; one per group How you look at it; several per group, each from one declared worldview Boundary is an existing unit such as an office, committee or division Boundary cuts across the organization chart Check Multiple choice Which pairing matches the two candidates the deck names? PT: "a system to turn unallocated resources into allocated ones"; IB: the school's mission statement IB: "a system to turn unallocated resources into allocated ones" (Ch.2, p.44); PT: the school's mission statement modelled as a root definition (Ch.4, p.138) Both are primary-task Both are issue-based Allocating resources cuts across units (an issue-based boundary), while a school's mission statement is the stated job of one unit — the school (primary-task). True / False Primary-task models are wrong, so a group should avoid them. True False They are "not wrong" — the risk is that they take the organization chart as given "and nobody notices." The advice is to never work with only one kind .

title: Lesson 3 · Do P, by Q, in Order to Achieve R
text: Lesson 3 · Do P, by Q, in Order to Achieve R Wed Oct 7 · Ch.2 p.39 · the formula for saying what a system is, in one sentence. P — what. Q — how. R — why. A system statement says what is done, how it is done, and why it is worth doing. Changing Q or R gives you a different system — even if P stays the same. The bus, from the deck A system run by the Town of Chapel Hill, its costs shared with Carrboro and the University, to bring students to campus (P), by running fare-free buses (Q), in order to get them to class without driving and needing somewhere to park (R). The transformation is in Q: fare-free buses, not simply buses. "Fare-free" is what makes this system this system. Q has to be a plausible how for P. The deck's counter-example: "Define health-care needs, by asking patients for their views" is not a plausible way to do what P says. By nurses judging and meeting each patient's needs on the ward By supplying the amount and quality of care set out in the contract By printing the hospital's annual report Q must be a plausible how for P. The first two are the deck's two versions of the nurse's system; printing a report is not a way of providing care. True / False If two statements share the same P, they describe the same system. title: Lesson 4 · T Changes One Entity
text: Lesson 4 · T Changes One Entity Mon Oct 12 · Ch.2 pp.40–41. T (transformation): an entity → the same entity, changed. • A fence → a painted fence • The health-care needs of Coketown citizens → the health-care needs of Coketown citizens met Not: one thing → a different thing (paint → a painted fence; doctors → healthy citizens). The test: say the thing on the left. Is the thing on the right the same thing, changed? Pass or fail? (the deck's four items, built from the PQR thread) The deck poses these for discussion without printing a key. The answers here apply the deck's test; check them against your skeptic's reading. ${mt4('match-t', [['pass','Pass — same entity, changed'],['fail','Fail — a different thing']], ['IT resources → efficient internal communication', 'Students at risk of graduating late → students on track to graduate on time', 'Career events and referrals → hired candidates', 'Research opportunities announced in three places → research opportunities announced in one place'], ['fail','pass','fail','pass'])} Practice True / False "Doctors → healthy citizens" is a valid T. True False False. Doctors are one thing and healthy citizens are another; T must change one entity. Multiple choice Which is a valid T (not from the slides)? Unread messages → the same messages, read A budget → a satisfied department Teachers → learning Only the first keeps the same entity and changes it.

title: CATWOE, on the Bus
text: CATWOE, on the Bus Ch.2 pp.41–42. Root definition: A system owned by the Town of Chapel Hill, with costs shared by Carrboro and the University, to meet students' need to get to campus without a car, by running fare-free buses, in order to get them to class without driving and needing somewhere to park. Click a letter: T W A C O E Match each letter to its role ${mt4('match-cw', [['t','The change the system makes'],['w','The view that makes T worth doing'],['a','Those who carry out T'],['c','Those who benefit or are harmed'],['o','Those who could stop the system'],['e','Constraints the system takes as given']], ['T','W','A','C','O','E'], ['t','w','a','c','o','e'])} Select all that apply In the bus example, who is in C (customers)? Students (beneficiaries) Taxpayers who fund rides they never take (victims) Drivers, dispatchers and mechanics The roads as they are Check C: students (beneficiaries) and taxpayers (victims). Drivers, dispatchers and mechanics are A; the roads are E. Multiple choice Why is O the Town, Carrboro or the University? Each of them runs the buses day to day Each is a beneficiary Any one can withdraw its share O is whoever could stop the system — here, any of the three can withdraw its share.

title: Writing the Card
text: Writing the Card Mon Oct 12 · one card per system. Front, in this order T: ___ → the same ___, changed W: why anyone would want T A, C, O, E Back The root definition as one sentence: a system owned by O, to do T, by Q, in order to R Start with the ✗ system , the one nobody in the group holds The skeptic checks every T with the test before anyone writes W No metaphors. "Go the extra mile" cannot be modeled. What would count as this system working? title: Declaring a Worldview, and the Steelman
text: Declaring a Worldview, and the Steelman Mon Oct 12 · the steelman, this week. The steelman: argue for a view you don't hold, so that someone who holds it would sign. Not a good declaration "AI people." "The administration, who only care about funding." Anyone's name. A good declaration "Those in university leadership who think SDIS should build its programs around AI. They would say it is for preparing every student for work that AI is already changing, and for keeping a public school useful to the state that funds it." Declare one you do not hold and are not sympathetic to . Start from the PQR thread, or the three lines from 10/7. The tells — each costs points ${mt4('match-tells', [['sq','Scare quotes'],['tb','"They believe that"'],['ei','Explaining by interest']], ['Leadership wants the school to be “AI-driven.”','They believe that AI will change every career.','Leadership backs AI because it brings in state money.'], ['sq','tb','ei'])} Also: anything that makes a holder wince. Multiple choice What goes in the steelman (up to 1200 words)? A critique of the view, then your own A summary of the PQR thread Quotes from the reading about the view A root definition and CATWOE for the view as its holders would state it, plus one paragraph on what this view sees that yours does not Exactly those two parts. True / False Your readers answer by saying whether your steelman is persuasive. True False False. They answer: "Yes, I could sign this." or "No. This sentence stopped me: '…'"
